newsitem.title: UK: FORECAST-UK rates stuck until after election - poll.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST-UK rates stuck until after election - poll.

text.p: UK official interest rates have hit bottom, and will stick at the current 5.75 percent level until they are increased by the incoming government after the election, according to a Reuter poll.

Not one of the 20 economists surveyed on Thursday thought there was a chance of a rate change at next Monday's monthly monetary meeting between Chancellor of the Exchequer Kenneth Clarke and Eddie George, Governor of the Bank of England.

Strong retail sales and money supply figures have pointed to a very firm economic recovery, virtually squashing the view that the Chancellor may try to squeeze in another rate cut ahead of the election, which must be held by May 1997.
"The chancellor will be much happier having this strong economic growth and will be under little pressure to press for further interest rate cuts," said Simon Briscoe, UK economist at Nikko Europe.
"As the economy strengthens, there is much less of an argument to cut rates to prop it up," agreed Ernesto Ramirez, European economist at Bankers Trust.

While the minutes of the July 30 meeting revealed that George would prefer to see rates at 6.0 percent, they suggested that there would need to be signs of genuine inflationary pressure before Clarke would be persuaded to raise rates, said Ian Gunner, international economist at Chase Investment Bank.
That apart, political sensitivity ahead of the election will mean the Chancellor is likely to resist a rate hike at all costs, economists said.
All respondents except one believed the next rate movement would be upwards, probably in the second quarter of next year, with rates peaking at around 6.75 percent in 1997.
"The best time for a government to raise rates is soon after they come into office because then the electorate has a chance to get over it," said Ciaran Barr, economist at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell.
He is predicting a 50 basis point hike in the second quarter of 1997. Most economists surveyed expect a rise of 25 basis points.
"The move will be very sharp. The election is nine months away and Clarke is already under pressure," Barr added.
A dissenting view from the consensus came from analysts at DKB, who said Clarke could lop another 25 basis points off rates around the time of the November 26 budget.

"Inflation is low, sterling is firm and we could have a cautious budget that will be well received by the markets," said DKB's economist, Gerard Lyons. "But if he goes for tax cuts, a rate cut would be out of the question."
